q: Which Governance process produces the project charter?
explanation: Initiate Project or Phase officially authorizes the project by creating a project charter or similar document. Its outputs are the charter and the assumption log.

q: Which is an input to the Initiate Project or Phase process?
explanation: Inputs include the business documents (business case, benefits management plan), agreements, EEFs and OPAs.

q: What is the main output of the Integrate and Align Project Plans process?
explanation: This process consolidates and aligns all plan components into a unified project management plan.

q: How much planning detail does the PMBOK Guide recommend?
options: As much detail as possible for every activity, before any of the work starts
The same fixed level for every project
Enough to move forward appropriately, but not more detailed than necessary
explanation: The time spent planning should fit the circumstances: sufficient to move forward in an appropriate manner, but not more detailed than necessary.

q: A company needs a common commodity service that it does not provide itself, and wants to shift delivery risk to another party. Which sourcing decision fits best?
options: Insource, because control is always better
explanation: Outsourcing is often less expensive when goods or services are common, brings in missing expertise, and transfers delivery risk to the supplier.

q: Which technique is used in Plan Sourcing Strategy to decide whether work is done internally or bought from outside?
explanation: Make-or-buy analysis determines whether work or deliverables are better accomplished internally or purchased from outside sources.

q: Which process leads and performs the work defined in the project management plan and implements approved changes?
explanation: Manage Project Execution performs the planned work and implements approved changes, including corrective actions, preventive actions and defect remediation.

q: Which of the following are outputs of Manage Project Execution?
explanation: Outputs include deliverables, work performance data, the issue log and change requests. Reports come from monitoring and controlling; approved change requests are an input.

q: What is the difference between quality assurance and quality control?
options: There is none; the terms are interchangeable
Quality assurance concerns using project processes effectively; quality control concerns deliverables meeting specifications
Quality assurance is done by the customer; quality control by the sponsor
Quality assurance happens only at closing
explanation: Quality assurance is about using processes effectively (standards, compliance, audits). Quality control is about deliverables meeting defined specifications (testing, defects).

q: An independent reviewer checks whether the project team is following the organization's required procedures. This is:
options: A quality audit, part of quality assurance
Defect repair, as part of executing the work
explanation: Audits examine whether processes are being followed, which is quality assurance. Inspecting or testing a deliverable would be quality control.

q: A senior engineer 'just knows' from years of experience when a design will fail, but finds it hard to explain why. This is an example of:
explanation: Tacit knowledge is personal, embedded in a person's mind, experience-based and difficult to articulate. Explicit knowledge can be codified in words, pictures or numbers.

q: What is the best way to share tacit knowledge within a project?
options: Write it in the project charter
Email a procedure to the team
Through conversation and interaction, such as mentoring and face-to-face work
explanation: Tacit knowledge is shared through conversations and interactions: mentoring, team building, face-to-face work and storytelling, in a trusting environment.

q: When should lessons learned be captured?
options: Only at the end of the project
Throughout the project and at its closure
Only when the project fails or is cancelled
explanation: Managing knowledge involves more than obtaining lessons learned at the end. Teams decide how and when lessons learned and retrospectives are conducted throughout the project.

q: Which process tracks, reviews and reports overall progress and produces work performance reports?
explanation: Monitor and Control Project Performance takes work performance information and produces work performance reports, change requests and forecasts.

q: A team is measured only on the number of features delivered, so it starts producing many small, low-value features. Which measurement pitfall is this?
explanation: The Hawthorne effect: the act of measuring something influences behavior. Measuring only output volume encourages volume over value.

q: A dashboard shows total website page views, which keep rising but do not help anyone decide anything. This is:
explanation: A vanity metric shows data but does not provide useful information for making decisions.

q: In a predictive project, when do changes start to be formally controlled?
options: From the first day of the project
explanation: In predictive approaches, changes are not formally controlled until baselines are established. After that, all changes go through the formal process.

q: A stakeholder asks the project manager to add a feature after the scope baseline is approved. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Add the feature to keep the stakeholder happy
Refuse, because the baseline is fixed
Document the request and assess its impact on schedule, cost and other aspects
Ask the team to work overtime
explanation: Changes should be documented and analyzed for impact, including schedule and cost, before a decision is made by the designated person or change control board.

q: What is the role of a change control board (CCB)?
options: To review, evaluate, approve, defer or reject changes, and record and communicate the decisions
explanation: The CCB is a formally established group responsible for reviewing, evaluating, approving, deferring or rejecting changes, and documenting and communicating its decisions.

q: How are changes typically managed in an adaptive project?
options: Through a formal change control board that reviews and signs off every single item
Through backlog management: the change becomes a backlog item and is prioritized
explanation: In adaptive approaches a proposed change is recorded as a product backlog item, its impact is analyzed and it is prioritized. Low priority means deferred; not added means rejected.

q: A project is cancelled halfway because funding was withdrawn. Which statement is correct?
options: No closing is needed for a cancelled project
Close Project or Phase still applies, including documenting the reasons for termination
The project manager should keep the whole team working as planned until instructed otherwise
explanation: Close Project or Phase finalizes both successful and unsuccessful projects, and includes investigating and documenting why a project was terminated early.

q: Which is a required input before a project can be closed normally?
explanation: Accepted deliverables are an input to Close Project or Phase. Closing confirms that deliverables were delivered and formally accepted by the customer.

q: Which of the following is an output of Close Project or Phase?
options: Final report and transition of the final product, service or result
explanation: Outputs include the final product, service or result transition, the final report, lessons learned register updates and organizational process asset updates.
